primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the pearl primarily symbolizes the kingdom of heaven (and by extension salvation, Christ, or the gospel) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing value — something worth surrendering everything else to obtain. This derives chiefly from Jesus' Parable of the Pearl of Great Price.
primary_basis: Matthew 13:45-46 (Parable of the Pearl of Great Price: the merchant sells all he has to buy the one pearl of great value)
Matthew 7:6 ('do not cast your pearls before swine' — pearls as sacred truth or the precious things of God)
Revelation 21:21 (the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem are each a single pearl, associating pearls with heavenly glory and entrance into God's presence)

alternatives.meaning: The reversed reading of Matthew 13:45-46: Christ is the merchant and the pearl is the Church or the redeemed believer, purchased by Christ at the cost of everything (his life). Widely taught in evangelical and dispensational circles (e.g., popularized in older dispensational commentary traditions).
basis: 1 Corinthians 6:20 / 1 Peter 1:18-19 (bought with a price, cited in support of Christ as the purchaser)
Ephesians 5:25 (Christ gave himself for the church)

alternatives.meaning: Pearls as sacred truth, doctrine, or the gospel message that must not be profaned or offered to the contemptuous — from 'pearls before swine.' Often treated as a distinct application rather than a competing definition.
Pearls as worldly luxury, wealth, and ostentation — a negative or cautionary symbol, especially in association with Babylon the harlot and warnings about adornment.

Patristic/allegorical readings identifying the one pearl specifically with Christ himself (sometimes linked to legends of the pearl's virgin birth from the oyster, used as an image of the Incarnation, e.g., in Ephrem the Syrian and other early writers).
basis: Matthew 13:45-46 as allegorized by church fathers (Origen, Ephrem the Syrian, Clement of Alexandria)

alternatives.meaning: The pearl as the human soul or divine spark, as in the Gnostic 'Hymn of the Pearl' (Acts of Thomas); influential in history-of-religions scholarship but not part of orthodox Christian consensus.
basis: Hymn of the Pearl in the Acts of Thomas (extra-biblical)

notes: There is a recognizable mainstream consensus that the pearl's central symbolic function is 'that which is of supreme value' — most commonly the kingdom of heaven/salvation per Matthew 13:45-46. However, the direction of the parable's allegory is genuinely disputed: the historically dominant reading makes the seeker the disciple and the pearl the kingdom, while a substantial popular tradition reverses it (Christ as merchant, believer/church as pearl). The negative usage (pearls as luxury in Revelation and 1 Timothy) is contextual rather than a competing core symbol. Prominence labels reflect published commentary, sermon literature, and Bible dictionaries; no single authoritative body fixes the meaning.
